title: Teaching
text:
I teach the politics of the criminal legal system as a subject students can analyze rigorously and connect directly to their own communities. My signature course, The Politics of Police and Prisons in the U.S., is the only course on the criminal justice system in Michigan’s Political Science department, and it regularly fills to capacity with a waitlist. In 2025 I rebuilt the course around specifications grading, replacing letter grades with a mastery-based rubric that lets students revise and resubmit their work until it meets a clear standard. I adopted this model to shift students’ attention from chasing points toward genuinely mastering concepts, to reward intellectual risk-taking, and to prepare students for professional settings where work is judged against standards rather than scored. Student evaluations consistently place the course above school and college medians on clarity, respect, and interest in the subject.
I design my courses to move students from abstract analysis to direct engagement with political institutions. In Police and Prisons, students build a semester-long portfolio of projects, including concept maps and an Institutional Power Map that asks them to apply what they learn about courts, police, and prisons to the governance of their own hometowns. I bring practitioners and scholars into the classroom — among them a county sheriff, a former public defender, and faculty from allied fields — so that students see how the system operates in practice. Roughly a third of my assigned readings come from scholars of color and women, and my attendance and accommodation policies are built to support first-generation students, caregivers, and students with disabilities. These choices reflect my conviction that a demanding course and an inclusive one are the same course.
Beyond the classroom, I founded and direct the Violence and Policing Lab, which brings graduate and undergraduate researchers together around the PKAP dataset. Lab members contribute to coding and analyzing the data and, in return, receive sustained mentorship on their own research. We meet monthly for students to present dissertation chapters and independent projects and to receive feedback from me and their peers. The lab creates a structured intellectual community that bridges research training and mentorship, and it has become central to how I support the next generation of scholars. I also advise dissertations, mentor undergraduate researchers, and write extensively for students pursuing law school and careers in the criminal legal field.

title: Shea Streeter

Assistant Professor of Political Science · University of Michigan


I study why some acts of state violence become public movements — and why so many others never do.

Read the research   Explore the data

title: Shea Streeter
text:
About
I am a political scientist who studies race, police violence, and the politics of accountability in the United States. My research asks a question that scholarship has largely left unanswered: why do some police killings ignite protest and demands for justice while others pass in silence? I argue that the answer begins with families. The decisions that grieving families make in the aftermath of a killing — whether to mourn privately or to demand justice publicly — determine when private loss becomes public movement. This reframing changes how we understand the Black Lives Matter movement, revealing that campaigns for police accountability have been carried, in large part, on the labor of grieving relatives.
My book project, Private Tragedy, Public Movement: Families and the Demand for Police Accountability, develops and tests this argument. I draw on the Police Killings and Protest (PKAP) dataset, an original resource that documents more than 3,000 police killings and codes each for whether it produced protest. I pair that quantitative evidence with interviews and fieldwork among the families of people killed by police, a population that existing research has rarely reached. Together, these sources let me build a three-part theory of grievance, bandwidth, and broadcast that explains how a single death can become a national cause. I direct the Violence and Policing Lab at Michigan, where a team of graduate and undergraduate researchers helps build and analyze this evidence.
My earlier and ongoing work examines state violence and its political consequences from several angles. In the Journal of Politics, I showed that racial disparities in police killings persist even after accounting for the circumstances of each encounter. In Public Opinion Quarterly, my coauthor and I demonstrated that Americans’ judgments about police violence turn on whether they perceive the victim as deserving. In a working paper on the 2020 uprising, my collaborator and I find that a county’s prior protest experience, not its rate of police violence, best predicts whether residents mobilized after George Floyd’s murder. Across these projects, I trace how communities translate — or fail to translate — violence into political action.

The data. Much of my work builds on the Police Killings and Protest (PKAP) dataset, which I assemble and code with the Violence and Policing Lab. The interactive police-killings explorer lets you examine these cases yourself. Each row represents a real death; I present the data soberly and with explicit attention to its limitations.

title: Police Killings: Data Explorer
Police Killings: Data Explorer
text:
Methods & limitations
This section will be completed with the full dataset’s documentation. The Police Killings and Protest (PKAP) dataset records police killings in the United States, geolocates each case, and — in its complete form — codes each for whether it was followed by protest. The records shown here cover 2015 and 2016 and are compiled from public records and journalistic sources; my research team arbitrates each coding decision. Counts of police killings undercount the true total, because no comprehensive official record exists, and categories such as race, ethnicity, and armed status carry their own measurement uncertainty. I will state the full coverage window, sources, and coding rules here, and I will publish only the variables designated for public release. Because each record is a person who was killed, I ask that the data be used with corresponding care.

title: Research
text: My research explains how communities respond to state violence, and why those responses so often diverge. I combine an original dataset of police killings with interviews, fieldwork, and survey experiments to trace the path from a single death to collective political action. The work spans three strands: a book project on families and the demand for accountability, a set of published articles on racial disparities and public opinion in policing, and ongoing studies of the geography and dynamics of protest. My publications are also listed on Google Scholar.

title: Research
text:
Book project

Private Tragedy, Public Movement: Families and the Demand for Police Accountability In progress
This book explains why some police killings lead to protest while others do not by placing families at the center of the story. I argue that the decisions families make in the wake of police violence — whether to grieve privately or demand justice publicly — determine when personal loss becomes political mobilization. Drawing on the Police Killings and Protest (PKAP) dataset, interviews, and fieldwork, I develop and test a three-part theory of grievance, bandwidth, and broadcast. The project reveals that movements for police accountability have largely been borne on the efforts of grieving families, reshaping how we understand the Black Lives Matter movement and related mobilizations.

title: Research
text:
Peer-reviewed articles

Police Abuse or Just Deserts? Deservingness Perceptions and State Violence
Shea Streeter and Mackenzie Israel-Trummel Public Opinion Quarterly 86, no. S1 (June 2022): 499–522.
Whether Americans condemn an act of police violence depends heavily on whether they judge the victim to have deserved it. Using survey experiments, we show that deservingness perceptions shape public reactions to state violence and help explain why similar killings provoke sharply different responses.

DOI



Bringing Abolition In: Addressing Carceral Logics in Social Science Research
Jordie Davies, Jenn Jackson, and Shea Streeter Social Science Quarterly (August 2021).
Social science research can unintentionally reproduce the carceral logics it studies. We argue that taking abolition seriously as an analytic commitment reshapes how scholars frame questions about crime, punishment, and the state, and we offer guidance for research that does not reinscribe carceral harm.

DOI



Lethal Force in Black and White: Assessing Racial Disparities in the Circumstances of Police Killings
Shea Streeter The Journal of Politics 81, no. 3 (July 2019): 1124–1132.
Do racial disparities in police killings simply reflect differences in the circumstances of police-civilian encounters? I show that they do not: substantial racial disparities persist even after accounting for the situational context of each killing, pointing to the role of race itself in lethal outcomes.

title: Research
text:
Working papers & works in progress

Mobilization Readiness and the Geography of Protest in the 2020 Uprising Working paper
Shea Streeter and Arica Schuett Presented at the 2025 University of San Diego Center for American Politics Conference.
Why did some U.S. counties mobilize during the 2020 racial-justice uprising while others did not? Merging the Crowd Counting Consortium’s record of more than 10,000 protests with county-level data across all 3,100 U.S. counties, we introduce the concept of mobilization readiness — a community’s prior experience with collective action. We find that earlier left-leaning protest activity strongly predicted Floyd-era demonstrations, while local rates of police killings did not.
